---
title: "Scoring California's Proposition 40 billionaire tax: one model for the static, migration, and valuation assumptions"
author:
  - name: "Max Ghenis"
    affiliation: "PolicyEngine"
date: "September 18, 2026"
bibliography: references.bib
abstract: |
  Proposition 40, on California's November 3, 2026 ballot, would impose a
  one-time tax of 5 percent of the entire net worth of residents (as of January
  1, 2026) worth $1 billion or more, valued on December 31, 2026. Public
  estimates of its fiscal effect run from roughly $100 billion in revenue to a
  negative net present value once future California income tax losses are
  counted. This paper documents a PolicyEngine calculator that scores the
  measure person by person from current Forbes data and exposes each contested
  assumption as a setting inside one model, so that the Berkeley and Hoover
  estimates become two parameterizations of the same calculation. The analysis
  has two stages. The first defines the taxable base and computes one-time
  receipts. The second optionally adds future California income tax losses,
  which requires separate assumptions about which departures are legally
  effective and which are attributable to the tax. On the September 18, 2026
  Forbes snapshot, the baseline covers 269 people and yields $120.9 billion of
  one-time revenue. Treating every documented departure and contested
  residency claim as effective removes $30.7 billion of tax, leaving $90.2
  billion, and counting the present value of those movers' California income
  tax under a 2 percent income yield and a 3 percent real discount rate
  reduces the net present value to $10.2 billion; the income tax assumption,
  which published estimates place between $0.15 billion and $3.1 billion a
  year, decides the
  sign. Every figure in this paper is computed by the calculator's code from a
  dated snapshot.
---

# Introduction

California's Proposition 40, the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, has produced one of
the widest gaps in recent state tax scoring. Galle et al. [-@galle2025;
-@galle2026july] report a roughly $100 billion static score using Forbes data
and a 10 percent haircut for avoidance or evasion. Rauh et al. build a
person-level base, adjust the residency roster, model departures, and estimate
that the policy may have negative net present value once foregone California
income tax is counted [@rauh2026]. The Legislative Analyst's Office expects
revenue in the "tens of billions of dollars spread over several years" and a
"possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year" in income tax
[@lao2026prop40].

This paper documents a public calculator built at PolicyEngine
[@policyengine2026]. The calculator is one model with its own baseline: the
statutory base applied person by person, one residency standard applied to
everyone, and receipts and losses dated and discounted on the same clock. The
assumptions behind each published estimate are settings inside that model: the
billionaire base, contested residency claims, directly held real estate,
observed and modeled departures, California income tax exposure, payment
timing, growth, and discounting.

The paper's argument is narrow. The main disagreement is not about arithmetic
inside a shared model. It is about a short list of modeling choices. A useful
public model should therefore expose those choices directly rather than hide
them behind a single headline number.

# The measure and existing estimates

The measure qualified for the November 3, 2026 ballot as Proposition 40
[@sos2026]. It fixes residency on January 1, 2026 and values net worth on
December 31, 2026 [@ballot2026]. The tax is 5 percent of the entire net worth
of an individual worth $1 billion or more; for net worth below $1.1 billion
the rate falls by 0.1 percentage point for each $2 million of shortfall,
reaching zero at $1.0 billion (Revenue and Taxation Code section 50301(b) as
proposed). Real property held directly or through a revocable trust is
excluded from net worth; real estate held through a business is not. The tax
is due with the 2026 return, in 2027, either in full or in five annual
installments with a 7.5 percent nondeductible deferral charge on the unpaid
balance. Receipts go to a reserve fund that is legally separate from the
General Fund. The Legislative Analyst notes that if Proposition 41 or 42, on
the same ballot, receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition
40 "could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a
majority of voters", because a court could find that the measures conflict
[@lao2026prop40].

The Berkeley estimate takes the broadest and simplest approach. It uses 204
California billionaires from the October 17, 2025 Forbes list, reports $2.19
trillion of wealth, multiplies by 5 percent, and applies a 10 percent haircut
to reach a roughly $100 billion figure in Galle et al. [-@galle2025]. That is a static revenue
score. It does not separately model departures or future California income tax
losses. The authors' July 2026 update removes Larry Ellison as very likely a
Florida resident, adds 24 California residents who are not US citizens and
whom Forbes does not place in a state, and reaches $104 billion on a $2,307
billion base [@galle2026july]. Boll, Saez and Zucman [-@bsz2026] extend that
work: they estimate that California billionaires pay about $3 billion a year
in state income tax, score the measure at $89 billion to $128 billion across
four scenarios, and put the annual income tax loss from mobility at $0.15
billion to $0.56 billion.

Rauh et al. construct a narrower and more behaviorally responsive base
[@rauh2026]. Their paper adjusts the Forbes residency roster, adds an omitted
California billionaire, estimates directly held real estate, and treats
announced departures as evidence of migration response. They report a $94.2
billion no-behavior baseline, a $67.5 billion score after six announced
departures, and a preferred revenue range of roughly $35 billion to $46
billion once additional migration response is included. The
paper's Monte Carlo exercise yields a mean net present value of -$24.7 billion.
Their literature-implied calibration applies a semi-elasticity of 10.32 per
percentage point, which Walczak [-@walczak2026] and Boll, Saez and Zucman
[-@bsz2026] both trace to Brülhart et al.'s Swiss estimate for a permanent
annual wealth tax, to the measure's 5 percentage points, for a 51.6 percent
loss of the base; the authors themselves call a semi-elasticity of 12 to 13
"plausible and conservative" for a one-time tax that an interstate move
avoids. Galle et al. [-@galle2026response] object that this counts a
permanent behavioral response against one-time revenue; Rauh and Jaros
[-@rauhjaros2026] reply that taxpayers respond to the expected future tax
regime, of which a first levy is evidence. Walczak estimates an ongoing loss
of $3.5 billion to $4.5 billion a year in state revenue, of which $2.5 billion
to $3.1 billion is income tax; the rest is sales tax and economic spillovers.

Galle et al. argue, in the expert report and in their response to Rauh et al.
[-@galle2026july; -@galle2026response], that most publicly discussed
billionaire moves should not be treated as legally effective changes in
California domicile. They contend that
California residency is determined by a totality-of-ties analysis weighing
family, business, political, and social connections, that self-reported
relocations receive little weight in that analysis, and that the one-time
nature of the tax sharply limits the incentive to move. That position relies
on California's fact-intensive residency doctrine and on legal and economic
scholarship that treats tax-induced physical migration as limited relative to
paper income shifting [@bracamonte2021; Galle, Gamage, and Shanske -@moneymoves2025].

A separate concern is valuation. Forbes wealth is a public estimate, not a tax
filing. If reported values to the California Franchise Tax Board come in below
public Forbes values, or if market prices move materially before the valuation
date, both static and behavioral scores can shift even before any migration
response is added.

# PolicyEngine's scoring framework

The calculator is easier to understand when broken into two stages rather than
treated as one combined fiscal estimate.

The first stage defines the taxable wealth base and applies the statutory tax
rules to that base. This yields a one-time wealth tax score.

The second stage optionally adds future California personal income tax losses.
That stage requires extra judgments that are not needed for the wealth tax
score alone: which departures are legally effective, which departures occur
early enough to matter for the one-time tax, and what share of observed or
modeled migration should be attributed to the tax itself.

## The tax base

The measure taxes people who were California residents on January 1, 2026 on
their net worth on December 31, 2026. The calculator therefore keeps two
lists apart. The residency roster is the set of people Forbes placed in
California on January 1, 2026. The valuation is the latest Forbes estimate
for each of them, wherever Forbes places them now. Six roster members Forbes
now places in another state keep a current valuation and stay in the base.
Nine roster members Forbes no longer lists anywhere, worth $24 billion when
last listed, are carried at the last positive value in the stored daily Forbes
history: Forbes drops people for several reasons, death among them, and
several of the nine were last listed well above $1 billion, so absence from
the list says nothing about net worth. People on Forbes's California list today who were not on its
January 1 list are added, with their January 1 residency assumed; on the
September 18, 2026 snapshot there are 56 people in this group holding $264
billion. The join knows list membership and nothing else. The January 1 list
is rebuilt from per-person Forbes histories, so it lacks anyone Forbes added
to its real-time list later, most of them with the annual list in March 2026,
and anyone whose state Forbes left blank that day. The group therefore mixes
people who crossed the threshold during 2026 with people who were billionaires
and residents all along. Five people on the current California list are under $1
billion once directly held real estate is removed and owe nothing. Names are
joined on a normalized key, because Forbes adds and drops "& family" from
display names.

One roster member is excluded from every base. Forbes lists Larry Ellison in
Manalapan, Florida, and both Galle et al. [-@galle2026july] and Rauh et al.
[-@rauh2026] now exclude him. A second person Rauh et al. add to their base,
David Sacks, is not on the Forbes list at all and so is outside a Forbes-based
roster; his reported departure is the sixth in their Table 6, which is why
five of the six are offered as adjustments below.

The baseline keeps everyone else on the roster and treats everyone in it as
a resident who keeps paying California income tax. Twelve documented
departure claims are offered as individual adjustments, each shown with its
evidence and source. Eight remove a person from the base as a non-resident on
January 1, 2026: two contested residency classifications from Rauh et al., and
six reported departures before January 1, five from Rauh et al.'s Table 6
plus Travis Kalanick, who has said on the record that he moved to Texas on
December 18, 2025. Four are reported or planned departures after January 1
(Rauh et al.'s Table 7, which marks three of them unconfirmed); those people
owe the wealth tax whatever happens next, so applying the claim keeps them in
the base, counts their future income tax as lost, and takes them out of the
pool the modeled migration response draws on. California domicile turns on a
closest-connection test, and none of these claims has been tested. Galle et
al. [-@galle2026response] argue that few of these people are likely to have
taken the steps a change of residency requires as a matter of law; Rauh et
al. treat all of theirs as effective. The calculator takes no position beyond
the baseline and reports what each one is worth.

Forbes leaves the state blank for most people who are not US citizens, so the
24 such California residents that Galle et al. count, holding about $150
billion, are absent from this base.

## Real estate exclusion and phase-in

The calculator applies the initiative text person by person. Directly held
real estate is excluded before the phase-in is computed. For billionaires whose
holdings are known in the Rauh dataset, the model uses those name-level values.
For missing cases, it imputes directly held real estate at 0.64 percent of net
worth, following the median-share approach described by Rauh et al.
[@rauh2026].

Both provisions are small in dollars today. Eight people on the September 18,
2026 roster fall between $1.0 billion and $1.1 billion, so the rate ramp costs
$0.28 billion against a flat 5 percent, and the real estate exclusion as
measured is worth $0.45 billion. The measured exclusion is a lower bound: the underlying data record
personal residences, and several fortunes built on real estate carry a zero.
The person-level structure matters for a different reason. Residency claims,
valuation, and income tax exposure all attach to individuals, and four people
hold 40 percent of the base.

## Behavioral erosion, migration, and timing

The model separates two channels that are often blurred in public debate.

The first is non-migration erosion of the wealth tax base. This is a reduced-
form haircut that lowers one-time wealth tax collections but does not generate
future California income tax loss.

The second is migration. Here timing matters. A clean implementation needs to
distinguish at least four cases: announced pre-January 1 departures, unannounced
pre-January 1 departures, post-January 1 but pre-vote departures whose effect
on wealth-tax liability depends on retroactivity litigation, and later
departures that can affect future California income tax without changing the
one-time wealth tax. The calculator separates the first three: announced
pre-January 1 departures as named adjustments, unannounced ones as a modeled
share or semi-elasticity, and later departures as an income-tax-only effect.
It does not model the retroactivity case; a post-January 1 mover always owes
the wealth tax.

Additional modeled migration can be entered either as a direct share of the
remaining base or via a migration semi-elasticity. In the second form the
calculator solves for the share of the base the response can still reach at
which observed plus modeled departures equal the finite-change mapping
`1 - exp(-epsilon times tau)`, so users can compare the paper's linearized
share-loss framing with the exact one.

A semi-elasticity estimated on a permanent annual wealth tax does not map
directly onto a one-time levy. A one-time 5 percent tax has the same present
value as a permanent annual tax of 5 percent times the discount rate, or 0.075
to 0.225 percentage points a year at real rates of 1.5 to 4.5 percent; at a
semi-elasticity of 10.32 that implies a base loss of 0.8 to 2.3 percent rather
than 51.6 percent. The larger figure follows if taxpayers expect the levy to
recur at the full rate indefinitely. Expected recurrence is therefore the
parameter in dispute, and the calculator's migration input should be read as
a statement about it.

This distinction is central to interpreting the Berkeley and Hoover estimates.
The Berkeley score embeds a reduced-form haircut in a static wealth tax
estimate. Rauh et al. model behavioral response primarily through migration,
which simultaneously lowers wealth tax collections and raises the present value
of lost California income taxes.

## California income tax loss

The current calculator maps California income tax loss through PolicyEngine's
California income tax model rather than directly reproducing Rauh's Franchise
Tax Board-based estimate. Annual California-taxable income is modeled as a
share of taxed wealth, and California income tax is then estimated from a
precomputed lookup at billionaire-scale incomes.

This is an explicit methodological choice, not a replication claim. Rauh et
al. estimate a $3.3 billion to $5.8 billion annual California personal income
tax contribution from the relevant billionaire cohort using a Pareto-tail fit
to Franchise Tax Board data, and back out an implied income yield on wealth of
1.3 to 2.3 percent [@rauh2026]. The PolicyEngine implementation instead uses a
structural income-to-tax mapping. The benefit is consistency across scenarios.
The cost is that the Hoover assumption set in the calculator is best
understood as Rauh-calibrated rather than as a direct FTB-data implementation.
The default income yield of 2 percent sits inside Rauh et al.'s implied range,
but this roster is larger than theirs: at 2 percent the baseline cohort pays
$6.4 billion a year, above their $3.3 billion to $5.8 billion and about double
the $3 billion a year that Boll, Saez and Zucman [-@bsz2026] measure for 2019
to 2025 ($4.3 billion in 2025). Boll, Saez and Zucman do not report an income
yield. They report California income tax of about 0.2 percent of wealth for
the group and 0.07 percent for the top four, which at the 13.3 percent top
rate imply yields near 1.5 and 0.5 percent, and one direct ratio: fiscal
income equal to 0.38 percent of public stock wealth for Page, Brin, and
Zuckerberg, whose wealth is mostly unrealized gains and who account for most
of the wealth in the reported departures. A single yield therefore overstates
the income tax at stake from the largest movers.

More importantly, any California income tax module embeds a causality
assumption. Once a departure is included in the PIT-loss calculation, the
calculator is effectively attributing that future income tax loss to the tax
episode. That is a much stronger claim than simply observing that a billionaire
left the state. The calculator therefore presents California income tax
effects as an optional second stage after the wealth tax base is defined, with
its own settings for timing, legal effectiveness, and causal attribution.

## Discounting and payment timing

Cash flows are indexed in years from 2026, the valuation year. The tax is due
with the 2026 return, and the measure contemplates estimated payments in April
2027 and final payments in October 2027, so the first receipt arrives in year
one; the first lost income tax return is filed in the same year. With stage
two off, the calculator reports nominal receipts, as a budget table would.
With stage two on, both legs move to present value as of 2026.

Two growth rates do different jobs and are set separately. Nominal growth of
wealth from the snapshot to December 31, 2026 scales the tax base. Real
growth of the movers' income tax stream, together with the real discount
rate, sets the spread $r - g$ of the perpetuity; the default of zero growth
and a 3 percent discount rate is Rauh et al.'s central case, and their 1.5
percent and 4.5 percent cases are one setting away.

Installments carry a 7.5 percent charge on the unpaid balance. Per $100 of
liability they return $115 in nominal receipts, and because the charge exceeds
any plausible discount rate they are worth more to the state in present value
than the lump sum.

# What the calculator shows

All figures use the Forbes snapshot for September 18, 2026 and are written by
`scripts/paper_numbers.mjs`; a test fails if any figure in this text differs
from what the code computes.

The baseline covers 269 people with combined net worth of $2,434 billion and
yields $120.9 billion of one-time revenue, or $108.8 billion after a 10
percent erosion haircut of the kind Galle et al. apply.

Applying all twelve documented departure claims removes $30.7 billion of tax,
leaving $90.2 billion from 261 people. Two people, Larry Page and Sergey
Brin, account for most of that difference.

Stage two on the same scenario: with a 2 percent income yield, full
attribution of the movers' income tax to the measure, a 3 percent real
discount rate, no growth, no return migration, and a perpetual horizon, the
movers' California income tax is $2.32 billion a year. Receipts are worth
$87.6 billion in present value and the lost income tax $77.4 billion, for a
net present value of $10.2 billion. At the Legislative Analyst's ceiling of $1
billion a year the same base nets $54.3 billion; at Walczak's $3.1 billion of
income tax it is -$15.4 billion. Within this model the income tax assumption
decides the sign.

The Berkeley and Hoover starting points in the calculator apply those papers'
assumptions to this roster. They do not reproduce the papers' rosters: Galle
et al.'s includes non-citizen residents that Forbes does not place in a
state, and Rauh et al.'s is fixed at the 2025 Forbes list, which the
calculator holds as its October 17, 2025 snapshot.

# Why the estimates differ

Scoring both sets of assumptions inside one model, on the same people and the
same data, turns the disagreement into arithmetic. On the September 18, 2026
snapshot the Berkeley assumptions give a net present value of $106.1 billion
and the Hoover assumptions give -$77.4 billion. Five assumptions separate
them. Neither figure is the paper's own: the Berkeley roster adds non-citizen
residents Forbes does not place in a state, and Rauh et al. score a smaller
2025 list with fewer named movers and a smaller income-tax base, which is why
their published mean of -$24.7 billion sits well above this model's reading
of their assumptions. Because assumptions interact, the value of each depends
on the order in
which they are applied, so the table reports Shapley values: each assumption's
marginal effect averaged over every ordering. The contributions sum exactly to
the gap. The last column gives the smallest and largest marginal effect across
orderings.

| Assumption | Worth ($ billions) | Range across orderings |
|---|---|---|
| Further migration before valuation | -$80.8 | -$172.0 to -$27.9 |
| Movers' future income tax | -$76.1 | -$134.6 to +$0.0 |
| Residency: documented departures | -$34.7 | -$107.3 to -$0.2 |
| Avoidance and valuation haircut | +$8.2 | +$5.7 to +$11.8 |
| Real estate exclusion and growth to valuation | -$0.1 | -$0.4 to +$0.4 |

: Bridge from the Berkeley assumptions to the Hoover assumptions, net present value as of 2026 {#tbl-bridge}

Three assumptions carry the gap, and all three concern migration: whether
reported departures before January 1, 2026 are legally effective, how much
more wealth leaves before the valuation date, and how much California income
tax the movers would otherwise have paid. The last two interact, which is why
their ranges are wide: each additional person assumed to leave also takes an
income tax stream. The avoidance haircut and the real estate exclusion, which
occupy much of the public argument about the static score, are small.

# Valuation remains the largest open issue

The largest remaining uncertainty may be the gap between public Forbes wealth
and the values that would actually be reported and defended for tax purposes.
Forbes wealth is fast-moving and intentionally approximate [@forbes2012]. Tax
reporting is slower, more adversarial, and shaped by different incentives. If
tax-reported values are systematically lower than Forbes values, then both the
Berkeley-style and PolicyEngine static scores are too high before migration is
considered.

Market movement between a public snapshot and December 31, 2026 adds a second
valuation risk. For fortunes concentrated in public stock, ordinary price
changes can move the base materially without any legal avoidance or migration.
Future versions of the calculator should separate that valuation wedge from the
migration question.

# Limitations and extensions

First, several provisions of the measure are not modeled: optional deferral
accounts for taxpayers whose tax exceeds their publicly traded assets, which
defer tax without interest until assets are distributed; the alternative
apportionment petition with its 25 percent floor; the presumptive valuation of
private businesses at book value plus 7.5 times average profits; limits on
deductible debt; aggregation of spouses; the flat 5 percent rate on certain
trusts; and the exemption of qualified pensions and retirement accounts, Roth
accounts up to $10 million, nonqualified deferred compensation, and tangible
personal property held outside California, which are negligible at Forbes
scale but unmeasured. The first of these changes the timing of receipts from
founders of private companies.

Second, the base omits California residents who are not US citizens, because
Forbes does not place them in a state. It also omits anyone the rebuilt
January 1, 2026 list does not contain, unless Forbes lists them in California
today; and it carries roster members Forbes has dropped at their last positive
stored value, which is a guess in both directions.

Third, the real estate data record personal residences, so the exclusion is a
lower bound.

Fourth, the calculator does not separate a valuation wedge between Forbes
estimates and values reported to the Franchise Tax Board, in either direction,
from the erosion haircut, and it holds wealth at the snapshot value unless the
user sets a growth rate to December 31, 2026.

Fifth, a single income yield is applied to everyone, which overstates the
income tax at stake from founders whose wealth is unrealized.

Sixth, the headline nets reserve fund receipts against General Fund income
tax. The measure makes those funds legally separate, and only the income tax
side enters the state's school funding guarantee.

Seventh, the model does not forecast the outcome of Propositions 41 and 42,
the validation action the measure provides for, or later litigation.

# Conclusion

Proposition 40 should not be summarized by a single number without showing the
assumptions underneath it. Reasonable choices about
the billionaire base, contested residency cases, directly held real estate,
migration, income tax exposure, valuation, and discounting are enough to move
the estimate from a roughly $100 billion static score to a much smaller figure
and, in some scenarios, to a negative net present value.

A transparent calculator is useful because it makes those choices visible. The
next stage of work should focus less on replacing one opaque point estimate
with another and more on improving measurement of the valuation base, the
contested residency base, and the California income tax exposure of the
affected cohort, while separating the one-time wealth tax score from the more
speculative question of later California income tax effects.
